findings.description: The reports bucket has no server_side_encryption_configuration block, so objects are stored using S3-managed keys only if a bucket policy/default exists; there is no enforced customer KMS key for sensitive report data.

The reports bucket defines no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block and no explicit acl, and force_destroy = true allows the entire bucket and its contents to be destroyed without protection, exposing data to accidental or malicious deletion.
No aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block is attached to the reports bucket to block public ACLs and policies, leaving it potentially exposed if an object or policy is later made public.
Financial ledger exports are stored without any server_side_encryption_configuration, so objects are not encrypted with a KMS key at rest.
The ledger exports bucket has versioning disabled, so deleted or overwritten ledger records cannot be recovered and tampering may go undetected.
Model artifacts are stored with no server_side_encryption_configuration block and no bucket key/KMS configuration, exposing artifact data at rest.
No public access block is configured for the model artifacts bucket, so public ACLs or policies could expose internal model data.
Operational runbooks are stored without server_side_encryption_configuration, leaving potentially sensitive infrastructure documentation unencrypted at rest.
The audit bucket uses the legacy acl = "log-delivery-write" canned ACL and has no aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block, so log delivery ACLs could be abused to expose or overwrite audit records.

The vendor roster object is uploaded to the reports bucket without specifying server-side encryption settings, so the containing bucket's unencrypted default applies to potentially sensitive vendor data.
